MUJAHID:v2p788/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p788/r1.speaker: علي
MUJAHID:v2p788/r1.claim: Ali says al-ma'un is the obligatory alms.

MUJAHID:v2p788/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p788/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
MUJAHID:v2p788/r2.claim: Ibn Masud says it is refusing to lend household tools such as an axe, bucket, or pot, items people commonly share.

MUJAHID:v2p788/r3.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p788/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
MUJAHID:v2p788/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says al-ma'un means household furnishings.

MUQATIL:107:1-7/r8.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:107:1-7/r8.speaker: author
MUQATIL:107:1-7/r8.claim: Muqatil identifies al-māʿūn as obligatory alms and says the Quraysh usage of the word means water.

MUQATIL:107:1-7/r9.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:107:1-7/r9.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
MUQATIL:107:1-7/r9.claim: A report from the Prophet identifies al-māʿūn as a needle, water, fire, and similar household items that people withhold.

FARRA:v3p294#2/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p294#2/r6.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p294#2/r6.claim: Al-māʿūn is all customary kindness, including lending a bowl, pot, or axe.

FARRA:v3p294#2/r8.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p294#2/r8.speaker: علي
FARRA:v3p294#2/r8.claim: A second report from ʿAlī gives the same interpretation, identifying al-māʿūn with zakat.

FARRA:v3p294#2/r9.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p294#2/r9.speaker: بعض العرب
FARRA:v3p294#2/r9.claim: Some Arabs say al-māʿūn is water; a poetic line about a cloud pouring it is cited as evidence.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r1.speaker: علي
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r1.claim: Ali interprets the withheld small kindness as zakat.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets it as lending ordinary household items.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r3.speaker: ابن عمر
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r3.claim: Ibn Umar says it is charity and insists on that answer when told people differ.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r4.claim: Ibn Masud explains it as lending a cooking pot, axe, or bucket.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r5.speaker: ابن عمر
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p399#3/r5.claim: Ibn Umar also defines the ma'un as withholding a due right.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p540#5/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p540#5/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p540#5/r2.claim: Others say al-māʿūn means water and pasture.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p540#5/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p540#5/r3.speaker: الفراء
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p540#5/r3.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the word can mean water itself, citing a line in which a cloud pours māʿūn.

TUSTARI:107:7/r2.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:107:7/r2.speaker: قيل
TUSTARI:107:7/r2.claim: Another interpretation says al-maʿun means alms.

TUSTARI:107:7/r3.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:107:7/r3.speaker: author
TUSTARI:107:7/r3.claim: Al-maʿun also means wealth in the language of Abyssinia.

TAB-FULL:v24p666/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r1.claim: Maʿun is the benefit of any thing people possess; rainwater is also called maʿun. The verse describes people withholding benefits from others.

TAB-FULL:v24p666/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r2.claim: Al-Aʿsha's verse uses maʿun for the benefit supplied when rain falls, and another poet uses it for rain pouring from a cloud.

TAB-FULL:v24p666/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r3.speaker: عبيد الراعي
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r3.claim: A verse by Ubayd al-Raʿi uses maʿun for obedience and zakat, linking withholding it with neglecting praise of God.

TAB-FULL:v24p666/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r4.speaker: علي
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r4.claim: Ali, in reports transmitted by Mujahid, interprets maʿun as zakat.

TAB-FULL:v24p666/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r5.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v24p666/r5.claim: Mujahid also glosses maʿun as zakat.

TAB-FULL:v24p668/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p668/r1.speaker: علي
TAB-FULL:v24p668/r1.claim: Ali's interpretation, transmitted through Mujahid, is that maʿun is obligatory charity or zakat.

TAB-FULL:v24p668/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p668/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
TAB-FULL:v24p668/r2.claim: Ibn Umar interprets maʿun as zakat, the right owed on wealth, and rejects Ibn Masud's interpretation as loaned household items.

TAB-FULL:v24p670#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p670#2/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v24p670#2/r2.claim: Ibn Masud says maʿun includes household implements people lend one another, such as an axe, pot, or bucket.

TAB-FULL:v24p670#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p670#2/r3.speaker: أصحاب محمد
TAB-FULL:v24p670#2/r3.claim: A report says the Prophet's Companions spoke of maʿun as the axe, pot, and bucket that people need and share.

TAB-FULL:v24p673/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p673/r1.speaker: أصحاب النبي
TAB-FULL:v24p673/r1.claim: The Prophet's Companions identify maʿun as commonly shared household items such as an axe, bucket, and pot.

TAB-FULL:v24p673/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p673/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v24p673/r2.claim: Ibn Masud says maʿun is a pot, axe, and bucket, or other similar household things people use among themselves.

TAB-FULL:v24p675/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p675/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود
TAB-FULL:v24p675/r1.claim: Ibn Masud interprets maʿun as everyday items people lend among themselves, including an axe, pot, and bucket.

TAB-FULL:v24p675/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p675/r2.speaker: إبراهيم
TAB-FULL:v24p675/r2.claim: Ibrahim says maʿun is the loan of people's household implements, such as an axe, pot, and bucket.

TAB-FULL:v24p675/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p675/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p675/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets maʿun as borrowing, with one report specifying an axe and bucket.

TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r1.speaker: عبد الله
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r1.claim: Abdullah reports that the Prophet's Companions understood withholding maʿun as refusing a bucket and similar useful objects.

TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r2.speaker: محمد بن كعب
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r2.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb interprets maʿun as recognized good or kindness.

TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r3.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r3.claim: Said ibn al-Musayyib says maʿun means money in the Quraysh dialect.

TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r4.speaker: الزهري
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r4.claim: Al-Zuhri also says maʿun means money in the Quraysh dialect.

TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p677#2/r5.claim: Al-Tabari prefers the general sense that they withhold useful things people lend one another and the rights God assigns to the poor and needy in their wealth, since the verse does not restrict what they withhold.

TAB-FULL:v24p677/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says maʿun means household goods, and another report says it is the loan people provide to one another.

TAB-FULL:v24p677/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas recounts that people differed over whether maʿun means zakat, obedience, or items lent to others.

TAB-FULL:v24p677/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r3.speaker: علي
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r3.claim: Ali combines withholding zakat with withholding lendable implements as meanings of maʿun.

TAB-FULL:v24p677/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r4.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r4.claim: Said ibn Jubayr says maʿun is a loan or borrowed item.

TAB-FULL:v24p677/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r5.speaker: أبو مالك
TAB-FULL:v24p677/r5.claim: Abu Malik identifies maʿun as the bucket, pot, and axe.

ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r3.claim: Al-māʿūn means things that are useful.

ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r4.claim: In pre-Islamic usage, māʿūn included any useful item, even an axe, bucket, pot, or fire striker—anything useful, little or much; al-Aʿshā’s poem uses the word māʿūnihi.

ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r5.speaker: الأعشى
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r5.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s line witnesses māʿūn as a useful possession or provision offered generously.

ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r6.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r6.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r6.claim: In Islam, māʿūn is said to mean zakat and obedience; al-Rāʿī’s verse mentions people withholding their māʿūn and neglecting the declaration of God’s oneness.

ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r7.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r7.speaker: الراعي
ZAJJAJ:v5p367#2/r7.claim: Al-Rāʿī’s poem uses māʿūnahum while describing people who withhold it and neglect tahlīl, supporting the gloss of ritual obligation and obedience.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r1.speaker: الزهري
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r1.claim: Al-Zuhri says al-maʿun means wealth in Quraysh usage.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r2.claim: The Prophet explains al-maʿun as useful household items such as pots, iron tools, and water.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r3.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r3.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says the verse describes hypocrites who pray publicly but withhold zakat when it is hidden.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r4.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r4.claim: Ikrimah says the foremost al-maʿun is zakat on wealth, while its smallest examples are a sieve, bucket, and needle.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r5.speaker: محمد بن كعب
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3469#2/r5.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb glosses al-maʿun as customary kindness.

NAHHAS:v5p297/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p297/r2.speaker: علي
NAHHAS:v5p297/r2.claim: A report through al-Suddī and ʿAbd Khayr identifies al-māʿūn as alms; similar but differing reports are attributed to Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbās.

NAHHAS:v5p297/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p297/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
NAHHAS:v5p297/r3.claim: He also explains al-māʿūn as the ordinary objects people lend one another.

NAHHAS:v5p297/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p297/r4.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v5p297/r4.claim: He reports that some Arabs use al-māʿūn for water and cites a poem describing a cloud pouring its rain.

NAHHAS:v5p297/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p297/r5.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p297/r5.claim: All these interpretations share the sense of a small, trifling thing one should not begrudge; the word derives from maʿn, a little thing.

SULAMI:v2p421#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p421#3/r1.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v2p421#3/r1.claim: Withholding means refusing to give wealth and life for God's pleasure; Abu Bakr gave everything and said he had left God and His Messenger for himself.

THALABI:v10p305/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p305/r10.speaker: محمد بن كعب والكلبي
THALABI:v10p305/r10.claim: They say al-maʿun is all customary kindness and help people exchange with one another.

THALABI:v10p305/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p305/r11.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب والزهري ومقاتل
THALABI:v10p305/r11.claim: They say al-maʿun means wealth in Quraysh’s dialect; al-Aʿsha’s poem supports this lexical meaning.

THALABI:v10p305/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p305/r6.speaker: علي
THALABI:v10p305/r6.claim: He identifies al-maʿun as obligatory alms; Ibn Umar, al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn al-Hanafiya, and al-Dahhak share this interpretation.

THALABI:v10p305/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p305/r7.speaker: عبد الله
THALABI:v10p305/r7.claim: He says al-maʿun means everyday tools such as an axe, bucket, cooking pot, and similar useful items.

THALABI:v10p305/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p305/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p305/r8.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas through Saeed ibn Jubayr interprets al-maʿun as borrowed goods and household utensils.

THALABI:v10p305/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p305/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p305/r9.claim: Through Atiyya, Ibn Abbas is also said to interpret al-maʿun as obedience.

THALABI:v10p306/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p306/r1.speaker: الفراء
THALABI:v10p306/r1.claim: He cites an Arab expression in which al-maʿun means obedience and compliance, illustrated by an unknown poet’s verse.

THALABI:v10p306/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p306/r2.speaker: الفراء
THALABI:v10p306/r2.claim: He also reports that some Arabs use maʿun for flowing water.

THALABI:v10p306/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p306/r3.speaker: قطرب
THALABI:v10p306/r3.claim: He derives the word from scarcity: maʿun names alms, charity, and kindness because they are a small part of much wealth.

THALABI:v10p306/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p306/r4.speaker: قيل
THALABI:v10p306/r4.claim: Another view says al-maʿun means things that must not be withheld, such as water, salt, and fire.

THALABI:v10p306/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p306/r5.speaker: النبي
THALABI:v10p306/r5.claim: In a report from Aisha, the Prophet says water, salt, and fire should not be withheld; sharing fire or salt earns the equivalent of what is cooked or seasoned, and giving water is likened to freeing sixty people or saving a life.

THALABI:v10p306/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p306/r6.speaker: الراعي
THALABI:v10p306/r6.claim: His poem describes a people who do not withhold their help or the confession of God’s oneness.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p350#2/r25.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p350#2/r25.speaker: علي، ابن عمر، الحسن، عكرمة، قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p350#2/r25.claim: These authorities say al-ma'un is the obligatory alms; al-Ra'i's poem continues as evidence in the next source segment.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r1.speaker: الراعي
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r1.claim: Al-Ra'i's poem illustrates interpreting al-ma'un as the due zakat in people's wealth.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r2.speaker: محمد بن كعب
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r2.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka'b says al-ma'un is recognized good conduct.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says it is obedience.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r4.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب، الزهري
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r4.claim: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhri say the Qurayshi word means property.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r5.speaker: الأعشى
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r5.claim: Al-A'sha's verse shows al-ma'un can mean water when needed, as in flowing water.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas says it is the everyday items people lend one another, such as a bucket, cooking pot, or axe; this is transmitted as an early report.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r7.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r7.claim: Abdullah ibn Umar says it is withholding what is due.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r8.speaker: الطبري، ابن عيسى
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r8.claim: Al-Tabari and Ibn Isa take it as the yield or useful benefit of wealth, derived from a word for something little.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p353/r9.claim: Mawardi also allows it to mean help that takes little effort and carries little burden.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p360/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p360/r4.speaker: ابن عباس وعلي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p360/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Ata, and Ali interpret al-maʿun as the alms due on their wealth.

WAHIDI-QT:107:7/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:107:7/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:107:7/r1.claim: Al-maʿun means alms and useful objects such as an axe, pot, water, or salt.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:107:1-7/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:107:1-7/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:107:1-7/r5.claim: The withheld aid includes zakat and useful items such as an axe, pot, water, or salt.

JISHUMI:v10p7555/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r1.speaker: ابن عباس، الحسن، عكرمة، قتادة
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ikrima, and Qatada classify the seven-verse sura as Meccan.

JISHUMI:v10p7555/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r2.speaker: الضحاك، الواقدي
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r2.claim: Al-Dahhak and al-Waqidi classify the sura as Medinan.

JISHUMI:v10p7555/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r3.speaker: مقاتل
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r3.claim: Muqatil says it is Meccan through the mention of the needy, with the remainder Medinan.

JISHUMI:v10p7555/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r4.speaker: النبي
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r4.claim: A report transmitted from Ubayy says reciting this sura brings God's forgiveness for one who pays zakat; no grading is given.

JISHUMI:v10p7555/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7555/r5.claim: After recounting favors to Quraysh, the sura marvels at their conduct despite Meccan security and provision, then their denial of the Prophet and his prophethood.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r10.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r10.claim: Mujahid interprets al-ma'un as a borrowed household item.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r11.speaker: عكرمة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r11.claim: Ikrima says its greatest instance is obligatory alms and its least is lending household goods.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r12.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r12.speaker: محمد بن كعب والكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r12.claim: They interpret al-ma'un as good conduct and help people exchange among themselves.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r13.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r13.speaker: قطرب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r13.claim: Qutrub derives al-ma'un from scarcity: zakat, charity, and kindness are called small contributions from a larger amount.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r14.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r14.speaker: قيل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r14.claim: Another view says al-ma'un means things it is impermissible to withhold, such as water, salt, and fire.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r7.speaker: علي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r7.claim: Ali interprets al-ma'un as the obligatory alms.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r8.speaker: ابن عمر والحسن وقتادة والضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r8.claim: Ibn Umar, Hasan, Qatada, and al-Dahhak also identify al-ma'un as zakat.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r9.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود وسعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p552/r9.claim: Ibn Masud, also reported by Said ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas, identifies al-ma'un as ordinary useful things such as an axe, bucket, or pot.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r12.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r12.speaker: الراعي
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r12.claim: Al-Rai's verse describes people failing to give their zakat and neglecting the declaration of faith, supporting the zakat sense of al-maun.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r13.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r13.speaker: ابن مسعود
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r13.claim: Ibn Masud interprets al-maun as ordinary household items people lend one another, such as an axe, pot, bucket, or fire striker.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r14.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r14.speaker: عائشة
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r14.claim: Aisha interprets al-maun as water, fire, and salt.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r15.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r15.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p809/r15.claim: Withholding such necessities is legally prohibited when someone borrows them from need, and is discourteous when there is no necessity.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r1.claim: The author calls withholding al-maʿūn a sign that they offer little benefit to God's servants, a blameworthy trait.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r2.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب وابن عمر
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r2.claim: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Ibn ʿUmar interpret al-maʿūn as zakāt.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r3.speaker: الراعي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r3.claim: Al-Rāʿī's verse is cited in support of the zakāt interpretation, describing people who withhold their al-maʿūn and neglect tahlīl.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود، الحسن، قتادة، ابن الحنفية، ابن زيد، الضحاك، ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r4.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and the named authorities define al-maʿūn as useful items people lend one another, such as an axe, bucket, vessels, or scissors.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r5.speaker: ابن المسيب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r5.claim: Ibn al-Musayyib says al-maʿūn means money in the Quraysh dialect.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r6.claim: A report transmitted by ʿĀʾisha says the Prophet named water, fire, and salt as things that may not be withheld; Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives no grading.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r7.claim: Some transmission routes add a needle and leaven to the items that may not be withheld.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r8.speaker: الفراء
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r8.claim: Al-Farrāʾ relates that some Arabs used al-maʿūn to mean water.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r9.speaker: ابن مسعود
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p528/r9.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says that in the Prophet's time they counted lending a pot, bucket, and similar items as al-maʿūn.

TABRISI:107:5-7/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:107:5-7/r12.speaker: علي، ابن عمر، الحسن، قتادة، الضحاك، أبو عبد الله
TABRISI:107:5-7/r12.claim: These authorities identify al-ma'un as the obligatory alms, a view also transmitted from Abu Abdillah.

TABRISI:107:5-7/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:107:5-7/r13.speaker: ابن مسعود، ابن عباس، سعيد بن جبير، النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
TABRISI:107:5-7/r13.claim: Ibn Masud, Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr interpret al-ma'un as commonly shared useful items such as buckets, axes, and pots, including things rarely withheld like water and salt; a raised report is also given.

TABRISI:107:5-7/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:107:5-7/r14.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABRISI:107:5-7/r14.claim: Abu Abdillah, in Abu Basir's report, defines al-ma'un as a loan, a good deed, lending household goods, and alms.

TABRISI:107:5-7/r15.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:107:5-7/r15.speaker: أبو عبد الله
TABRISI:107:5-7/r15.claim: Abu Abdillah says there is no blame in refusing to lend household goods to neighbors who break or damage them.

TABRISI:107:5-7/r16.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:107:5-7/r16.speaker: الكلبي
TABRISI:107:5-7/r16.claim: Al-Kalbi interprets al-ma'un as all good deeds.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r1.claim: Al-māʿūn includes household items such as a needle, water, fire, and an axe; a report traces this interpretation to the Prophet.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r2.claim: They share the household-utensil interpretation; Abū Ṣāliḥ also transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that it means every recognized kindness, even lending a pot, bowl, or axe.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r3.speaker: عكرمة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r3.claim: The warning is not about refusing a small household item alone, but about hypocrites who pray to be seen, neglect prayer, and withhold such things.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r4.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r4.claim: In pre-Islamic usage and Islam, al-māʿūn means anything beneficial, such as an axe, pot, bucket, or fire drill.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r5.speaker: علي وابن يعمر والحسن وعكرمة وقتادة

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r8.speaker: محمد بن كعب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r8.claim: Another interpretation is kindness or customary good treatment.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r9.speaker: الفراء عن بعض العرب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p245/r9.claim: Another interpretation is water; al-Farrāʾ cites a line using al-māʿūn for rain cloud.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r1.claim: After discussing prayer, the passage follows by mentioning the withholding of aid.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r10.speaker: العلماء
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r10.claim: Scholars praise keeping extra household necessities to lend neighbors, rather than limiting oneself to the obligatory minimum.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r11.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r11.claim: Al-Farra reports an Arab usage equating “al-ma'un” with water and cites the line “يمج بعيره الماعون مجا” as evidence.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r12.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r12.claim: Water may be singled out because it is most precious when absent and commonplace when present; people in Hell first ask for it, and it is among the first pleasures of Paradise.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r13.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r13.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r13.claim: A fourth view defines “al-ma'un” as willing obedience, as in the saying “restrain your camel until it gives you obedience.”

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r2.speaker: أبو بكر وعلي وابن عباس وابن الحنفية وابن عمر والحسن وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة وقتادة والضحاك

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r3.speaker: أبي
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r3.claim: A report from Ubay says reciting Surat al-Ma'un brings forgiveness for one who pays zakat, which suggests that “al-ma'un” means zakat.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r4.claim: The placement after prayer supports the zakat interpretation, since zakat naturally follows prayer.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r5.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r5.claim: Most commentators say “al-ma'un” names ordinary useful items that people customarily lend and whose refusal marks bad character, such as an axe, pot, bucket, fire striker, sieve, or adze; the list also includes salt, water, and fire.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r6.claim: A report says three things may not be withheld: water, fire, and salt.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r7.claim: Ordinary examples include letting a neighbor bake in one's oven or store belongings at one's home briefly.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r8.claim: “Ma'un” is a diminutive thing, from “ma'n”; zakat is called this because a small fraction is taken from a larger holding, and customary borrowed tools also bear the name.

RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p108/r9.claim: On the everyday-items reading, the verse rebukes stinginess over small things, a trait of hypocrites; the author connects it to warnings about misers and those who withhold good.

RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r1.claim: Razi prefers the broadest meaning: every act of obedience that is easy to perform, since this interpretation is more beneficial.

RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r2.claim: The contrast is that prayer belongs to God and al-ma'un belongs to people: hypocrites display to people what is due to God and conceal from people what is due to them, reversing proper conduct toward both.

RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r3.claim: The explanation that God concealed the hypocrite's name is answered by saying Adam's lapse was named only after his death and coupled with repentance, as a lesson to his descendants.

RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r4.claim: Adam's small sin led to his expulsion from Paradise, so people should not expect entry after committing a major sin.

RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r5.claim: Naming Adam's lapse also honors him, since it was his only lapse and he repented with such repentance.

RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p109/r6.claim: In the closing prayer, Razi contrasts the present sura's hypocrites with the next sura's description of Muhammad: though short of Muhammad and his Companions in obedience, he prays that they remain unlike the hypocrites in evil and asks God's pardon.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r1.speaker: الثعلبي وابن ماجه
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r1.claim: Al-Tha'labi cites the water, fire, and salt report, which Ibn Majah records; Qurtubi says its chain is weak, and it is the twelfth interpretation.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r2.speaker: الماوردي
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r2.claim: Al-Mawardi suggests ma'un means assistance through an act that is small but treated as burdensome.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r3.speaker: عكرمة مولى ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r3.claim: Ikrima says that refusing one household object alone does not merit woe; the condemnation concerns combining neglected prayer, showiness, and stinginess with ma'un.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r5.claim: A sincere Muslim is unlikely to combine all three traits, though withholding a necessary aid, like abandoning prayer, earns a share of the rebuke.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7#2/r6.claim: Withholding assistance is reprehensible as a matter of good character only outside necessity.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r1.claim: The continuation of al-Rai poem identifies maun with zakat paid from wealth and condemns withholding it.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r10.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r10.claim: Ibn al-Arabi derives ma'un as a passive form from helping: aid supplies power, tools, and means that ease an undertaking.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r11.speaker: الأخفش
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r11.claim: Al-Akhfash cites a fluent Bedouin using ma'un for a camel's compliance and obedience.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r12.speaker: الراجز
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r12.claim: A rajaz poet uses ma'un for yielding or complying.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r13.speaker: عائشة
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r13.claim: Aisha asks what may not be withheld; the Prophet names water, fire, and salt, then describes the immense charity of sharing fuel, seasoning, and water.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas also says al-ma'un is a loaned household item.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r3.speaker: محمد بن كعب والكلبي
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r3.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Kalbi say al-ma'un means all customary good deeds people exchange.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r4.claim: Another view identifies al-ma'un as water and pasture; a further view restricts it to water.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r5.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r5.claim: Al-Farra heard Arabs use ma'un for water and cites a poem describing a cloud pouring it.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r6.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r6.claim: Ibn Umar says al-ma'un means withholding what is due.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r7.speaker: الطبري وابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r7.claim: Al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas take al-ma'un as the yield or benefit from property, deriving it from ma'n, something small.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r8.speaker: قطرب
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r8.claim: Qutrub derives ma'un from scarcity: Arabs say a person has no little thing, and zakat is a small amount drawn from much wealth.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r9.speaker: الجوهري
QURTUBI-FULL:107:1-7/r9.claim: Al-Jawhari says the word originally meant ma'una, with the alif replacing the feminine ending.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r4.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits Ibn Abbas's view that al-ma'un is obligatory alms; the intended person is a hypocrite who withholds it.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r5.speaker: علي ومالك
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r5.claim: Ali and Malik also identify al-ma'un as zakat.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r6.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r6.claim: Malik says a hypocrite prays only to be seen and does not regret a missed prayer, while al-ma'un is the zakat God imposed.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r7.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r7.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says hypocrites would not pray if prayer were as hidden from people as zakat.

QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r8.speaker: الزجاج وأبو عبيد والمبرد
QURTUBI-FULL:107:7/r8.claim: Al-Zajjaj, Abu Ubayd, and al-Mubarrad say the pre-Islamic maun covered every useful item, while in Islam it means obedience and zakat.

BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r2.claim: Al-maʿūn can mean the obligatory alms (zakāt).

BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r3.claim: Al-maʿūn can also mean things customarily lent for use.

BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r4.claim: The fa in the woe passage is consequential: neglect of the orphan already shows weak religion and deserves blame, so heedlessness of prayer, ostentation, and withholding zakāt merit it even more; prayer is religion's pillar, ostentation a branch of unbelief, and zakāt Islam's bridge.

BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r6.claim: Calling them “those who pray” in place of a pronoun signals their bad treatment of both the Creator and other people.

BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:107:6-7/r7.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that whoever recites Sūrat Araʾayta is forgiven if he pays zakāt; Bayḍāwī gives no grading.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p359#4/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p359#4/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p359#4/r7.claim: Al-maʿūn may mean the obligatory alms tax.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p359#4/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p359#4/r8.speaker: ابن مسعود
NASAFI-FULL:v4p359#4/r8.claim: Ibn Masud says al-maʿūn is what people commonly lend one another, such as an axe, pot, bucket, or fire striker.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p359#4/r9.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p359#4/r9.speaker: عائشة
NASAFI-FULL:v4p359#4/r9.claim: Aisha identifies al-maʿūn as water, fire, and salt.

QASHANI:107:7/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:107:7/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:107:7/r4.claim: They withhold useful help, money, and goods from selfishness and narrow interests; lacking love, justice, fear, and hope, they do not assist others and will not prosper.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r1.claim: Sahā means to neglect or leave something through heedlessness; māʿūn may mean any small thing from the root maʿn.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r2.claim: Other etymologies derive māʿūn from maʿūna with a compensating alif, or from the passive of aʿāna with a series of sound changes.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r3.speaker: أبو عبيدة والزجاج والمبرد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r3.claim: Abū ʿUbayda, al-Zajjāj, and al-Mubarrad say pre-Islamic māʿūn meant anything useful, from an axe or bucket to a cooking pot or fire striker; the verse by al-Aʿshā witnesses this sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r4.claim: Another reported interpretation gives māʿūn the sense of obedience in Islam.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r5.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r5.claim: Most commentators call the surah Meccan; Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatada say Madinan, while Hibat Allāh says its halves came down in Mecca and Medina.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p551/r6.claim: Since the previous surah recalled God's favors to Quraysh, this one threatens those who deny resurrection and recompense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p553/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p553/r8.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p553/r8.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī offers an alternative syntax joining fa-dhālika to the one who denies judgment, omitting the answer to araʾayta, and making the woe to praying hypocrites a description standing for their pronoun; generic singular carries a plural sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r13.speaker: ابن المسيب وابن شهاب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r13.claim: Ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Shihāb say that in Quraysh usage al-māʿūn means wealth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r14.speaker: الفراء عن بعض العرب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r14.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reports that some Arabs use al-māʿūn to mean water.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r15.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس وابن الحنفية والحسن والضحاك وابن زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r15.claim: They interpret al-māʿūn as things people lend one another, such as an axe, bucket, or household vessels.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r16.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r16.speaker: النبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r16.claim: A Prophetic report says that water, salt, and fire are things one may not withhold.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r17.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r17.speaker: النبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r17.claim: Some transmission routes add a needle and leaven to the things that should not be withheld.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r18.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r18.speaker: علي وابن عمر وابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r18.claim: ʿAlī, Ibn ʿUmar, and Ibn ʿAbbās also interpret al-māʿūn as zakat.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r19.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r19.speaker: الراعي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r19.claim: Al-Rāʿī’s poem supports the zakat interpretation by saying that the community should give its zakat from its wealth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r20.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r20.speaker: قطرب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r20.claim: Quṭrub derives the word from al-maʿn, meaning a small thing; zakat is called māʿūn because it is a small portion of much wealth, like other charity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r21.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r21.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r21.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says al-māʿūn means a loaned item.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r22.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r22.speaker: محمد بن كعب والكلبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r22.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Kalbī say al-māʿūn means all good deeds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r23.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r23.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r23.claim: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar interprets al-māʿūn as withholding what is due.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r24.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r24.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p554/r24.claim: Another reported interpretation of al-māʿūn is water and pasture.

SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r1.speaker: قطرب
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r1.claim: Qutrub derives ‘ma‘un’ as fa‘ul from ma‘n, ‘a small thing’, citing ‘ma-lahu ma‘na’ for someone with little property.

SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r2.claim: A second derivation makes it a passive participle of ‘a‘ana’; its original form would be ma‘wun, with metathesis and vowel change producing the attested form and pattern maf‘ul.

SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r3.claim: That derivation has three irregularities: a passive from form IV normally has the maf‘al pattern, it uses metathesis, and it changes an unvocalized weak letter to alif; the author calls comparison with ‘taba’ and ‘ṣama’ weak.

SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r4.claim: A possible answer to the final irregularity is that the wāw was vocalized before metathesis, as the reconstructed ‘ma‘wun’ suggests.

SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r5.claim: The preferred derivation is ma‘una, with alif replacing the feminine tā’; on this account ma‘un means anything people use and benefit from, such as an axe, bucket, or fire striker.

SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r6.speaker: الأعشى
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r6.claim: Al-A‘sha’s poem uses ‘ma‘unihi’ for useful provisions or resources; it is offered as poetic evidence for the preferred sense.

SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:107:7/r7.claim: The object of ‘yamna‘un’ is omitted because people or petitioners are understood, or because the point is to condemn withholding trifling things that everyone recognizes should not be denied.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r1.claim: The verse condemns refusing to lend useful objects whose substance remains and is returned; those who refuse these favors are even more likely to withhold zakāt and other devotions.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r2.speaker: علي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r2.claim: ʿAlī and many early authorities identify al-māʿūn as zakāt.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r3.speaker: الحسن البصري
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī says they pray to show off, do not regret missing prayer, and withhold the zakāt or charity of their wealth.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r4.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r4.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says they are hypocrites who perform the visible prayer but withhold the zakāt that was enjoined.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r5.claim: Ibn Masʿūd explains al-māʿūn as ordinary items people lend one another, such as an axe, cooking pot, and bucket.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r6.speaker: أصحاب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p495#2/r6.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports that the Prophet's Companions would say that al-māʿūn meant a bucket, axe, and cooking pot, necessities that people lend.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r1.claim: A report says every good deed is charity, and that in the Prophet's time they counted lending a bucket or pot as al-māʿūn.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r10.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r10.speaker: الزهري
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r10.claim: Al-Zuhrī says that in Quraysh usage al-māʿūn means wealth.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r11.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r11.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r11.claim: A strange report from Qurra ibn Damʿūs says the Prophet instructed delegates not to withhold al-māʿūn, explaining it as stone, iron, and water, including cooking pots and axes.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r2.claim: Ibn Masʿūd identifies al-māʿūn as loaned household goods: pots, scales, and buckets.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and other early authorities explain al-māʿūn as household belongings lent to others.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r4.claim: A separate report from Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the phrase as meaning that the owners have not yet come for their belongings.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports disagreement: some say al-māʿūn is zakāt, some obedience, and others lending items.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r6.speaker: علي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r6.claim: ʿAlī is also reported to explain al-māʿūn as refusing people an axe, cooking pot, or bucket.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r7.speaker: عكرمة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r7.claim: ʿIkrima says the head of al-māʿūn is zakāt, while its least forms include a sieve, bucket, and needle.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r8.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r8.claim: Ibn Kathīr approves ʿIkrima's synthesis because it includes all reported views: the shared idea is refusing help through wealth or useful service.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r9.speaker: محمد بن كعب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p496/r9.claim: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb explains al-māʿūn as ordinary kindness, supported by the report that every good deed is charity.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p497/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p497/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p497/r1.claim: Ibn Kathīr calls the preceding report extremely strange and its Prophetic attribution rejected, noting an unknown narrator.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p497/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p497/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p497/r2.claim: A report cited from Ibn al-Athīr's Companion biography of ʿAlī al-Numayrī says a Muslim should greet another, return a better greeting, and not withhold al-māʿūn.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p497/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p497/r3.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p497/r3.claim: In the same report, the Prophet explains al-māʿūn as stone, iron, and similar useful things.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r7.speaker: أبو جعفر بن الزبير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r7.claim: He notes that people affiliated with Islam may push an orphan from his rights or fail to care for him, discourage feeding the poor, neglect prayer, show off, and withhold zakat or necessities.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r8.speaker: أبو جعفر بن الزبير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r8.claim: He reads these traits as those of a denier who expects no judgment, while observing that such acts can occur among Muslims without every person who commits them necessarily being a denier.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#2/r9.claim: The author compares this trait-based description to hadiths that call one with four specified traits a pure hypocrite and say a fornicator is not a believer while committing the act.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#s107/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#s107/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#s107/r1.claim: The surah is also called al-Din, Ara'ayta, and al-Takdhib; its purpose is to show denial of resurrection and recompense as the root of vile character and contempt for people's rights.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#s107/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#s107/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p541#s107/r2.claim: Its names clearly point to its theme on reflection: it directly forbids vice and indirectly calls people toward noble conduct.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r1.claim: These people may do lesser good ostentatiously but are so dominated by greed that they cannot even show off by giving a trivial benefit; the best people in God's sight benefit His dependents most.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to interpret al-ma'un as a loan or lending; al-Harawi records this through Abd al-Haqq al-Ishbili's book.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r11.speaker: ابن جرير
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r11.claim: Ibn Jarir says the root meaning of al-ma'un is the benefit of any thing.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r12.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r12.claim: Withholding al-ma'un shows extreme denial: these people disdain a major religious pillar while magnifying tiny worldly matters; the cause is denial of recompense.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r13.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r13.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r13.claim: The ending returns to the beginning because denial of judgment breeds neglect of people and obedience to God, contempt for the weak, and ostentation; the surah urges the opposite, noble character.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r14.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r14.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r14.claim: Those who withhold even trifles deserve to be denied al-Kawthar at the gathering, and the surah's final point echoes its opening.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r15.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r15.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r15.claim: The seven-verse al-Ma'un parallels seven-verse al-Anfal in number and in turning its ending back to its opening; al-Anfal expands the same lesson, so readers should notice the connection.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r2.claim: The imperfect verb 'withhold' suggests repeated behavior, and omission of its first object generalizes the withholding to everyone, even the highly esteemed.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r3.claim: Al-ma'un includes financial rights and small useful items, such as ordinary household objects people lend one another.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r4.claim: The threat of woe applies to withholding what must be given, including surplus pasture or water and zakat, as well as similar obligatory rights owed to the needy.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r6.speaker: بعضهم
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r6.claim: Some explain al-ma'un as a small thing, such as water or a loaned household item, or as zakat, which is small in relation to the wealth from which it is due.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r7.speaker: بعضهم
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r7.claim: Another reported interpretation takes al-ma'un to mean every gift or benefit.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r8.speaker: قطرب
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r8.claim: Qutrub derives ma'un as a fa'ul form from ma'n, meaning recognized kindness.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r9.speaker: أبو عبيدة
BIQAI-FULL:v8p544/r9.claim: Abu Ubayda says al-ma'un meant gifts and benefits in pre-Islamic times and zakat in Islam.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r1.claim: Al-Anfal 8:4 describes true believers as those who establish prayer and spend from God's provision, connecting with al-Ma'un's themes of prayer and giving.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r2.claim: The surah has twenty-five words; counting from the beginning of prophethood points to year twelve AH, when Abu Bakr had eliminated the apostates and zakat-refusers, exposing their earlier prayer and almsgiving as mere show.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r3.claim: Abu Bakr's campaigns ended in that year with the defeat of Banu Hanifa at Yamama, people of al-Nujayr in Kindah, and al-Aswad al-Ansi in Sanaa.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r4.claim: The twenty-five words plus the four-word basmala point to year sixteen AH: Arab polytheists, Christians, and Magians had left the peninsula, most converting and the rest going to Byzantine lands.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p545/r6.claim: Counting pronouns is unsuitable because the religion had become openly manifest and unobstructed; counting letters is also unnecessary after its public triumph became clear.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says maʿun is the loan of household goods.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r10.speaker: الضحاك وابن الحنفية
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r10.claim: Al-Dahhak and Ibn al-Hanafiyyah say maʿun means alms.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r11.speaker: محمد بن كعب
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r11.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says maʿun means good deeds or ordinary kindness.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r12.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that people differ: some interpret maʿun as alms, obedience, or a loan.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r13.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r13.claim: A final report from Ibn Abbas says these people had not yet appeared.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r2.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr defines maʿun as a loan.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r4.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r4.claim: Ali says maʿun is obligatory alms: they show off in prayer and withhold their alms.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r5.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r5.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says hypocrites perform the visible prayer but withhold the hidden alms.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas also identifies maʿun as alms.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r7.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r7.claim: Ibn Umar defines maʿun as wealth whose due has not been paid, and accepts Ibn Masud’s description of shared helpful goods as the same point.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r8.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r8.claim: Ikrima calls zakat the highest form of maʿun and lists a sieve, bucket, and needle as its smallest forms.

DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r9.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
DURR-FULL:v8p644#2/r9.claim: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib says maʿun means wealth in Quraysh usage.

DURR-FULL:v8p644/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r1.claim: Ibn Masud says maʿun includes the bucket, pot, and axe, objects people cannot do without.

DURR-FULL:v8p644/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r2.claim: Ibn Masud likewise defines maʿun as an axe, pot, bucket, and similar household tools.

DURR-FULL:v8p644/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r3.claim: Muslims borrowed these utensils from hypocrites, who refused them, and the verse was revealed.

DURR-FULL:v8p644/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r4.claim: The Prophet defines maʿun as items people help one another with, such as an axe, pot, and bucket.

DURR-FULL:v8p644/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r5.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r5.claim: The Prophet tells a delegation not to withhold maʿun and defines it as stone, iron, and water, including ordinary pots and tools.

DURR-FULL:v8p644/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r6.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r6.claim: The Prophet says a Muslim should not withhold maʿun; it includes stone, water, copper pots, and commonly used iron tools.

DURR-FULL:v8p644/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r7.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r7.claim: Ali reports that the Prophet says Muslims should greet one another, return something better, and not withhold useful items such as stone, iron, and water.

DURR-FULL:v8p644/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r8.speaker: أم عطية
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r8.claim: Umm Atiyya says the Prophet ordered them not to withhold maʿun, meaning things people share; the report is graded weak.

DURR-FULL:v8p644/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r9.speaker: أصحاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p644/r9.claim: Companions of the Prophet define maʿun as an axe, pot, and bucket.

BURSEVI:v10p404/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p404/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p404/r3.claim: Ma‘un comes from a word for something small; zakat is called ma‘un because one gives a small fraction of a larger amount.

BURSEVI:v10p404/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p404/r4.speaker: أبو الليث
BURSEVI:v10p404/r4.claim: Abu al-Layth says ma‘un means wealth in the Abyssinian language.

BURSEVI:v10p404/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p404/r5.speaker: برهان القرآن
BURSEVI:v10p404/r5.claim: Burhan al-Qur’an explains the repeated “those who are” as a grammatical necessity: the verse does not coordinate a verb directly with a noun, while repeating the phrase allows a verb to follow a verb.

BURSEVI:v10p404/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p404/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p404/r6.claim: Ma‘un means zakat, as suggested by its mention after prayer, or ordinary items people lend one another, such as tools, cookware, water, salt, and fire.

BURSEVI:v10p404/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p404/r7.speaker: عائشة
BURSEVI:v10p404/r7.claim: ‘A’isha asks what may not be withheld; the Prophet names water, fire, and salt, and says sharing fire or salt shares the food prepared with them, while giving water where none exists is like saving a life.

BURSEVI:v10p404/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p404/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p404/r8.claim: Withholding such necessities can be legally forbidden in an emergency and is poor manners outside an emergency; the verse rebukes the stinginess characteristic of hypocrites.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r1.speaker: علي ومحمد بن الحنيفة وابن عباس وابن عمر وزيد بن أسلم والضحاك وعكرمة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r1.claim: These authorities interpret al-ma'un as zakat; al-Ra'i's poetry is also cited in support.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r10.claim: The fa in fa-wayl marks consequence and the discourse escalates: if abandoning the orphan and failing to urge feeding are bad, neglecting prayer, showing off, and withholding zakat or even common loans are worse.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r11.claim: These vices characterize those who deny Judgment, so believers must avoid them; denial of the religion is the root of every sin.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r12.speaker: قيل
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r12.claim: One report identifies the person as Abu Jahl, who was guardian to an orphan but harshly drove away the unclothed child when he asked for his own property.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r2.speaker: محمد بن كعب والكلبي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r2.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Kalbi are cited for interpreting al-ma'un as customary helpfulness or a common good.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r3.claim: Ibn Mas'ud interprets al-ma'un as household items people lend one another, such as a cooking pot or axe; a report from Ibn Abbas is also cited by al-Diya and al-Hakim, who authenticated it.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r4.claim: Refusing to lend such things can be forbidden when someone is in need and blameworthy in good manners when there is no necessity; several Prophetic reports support the interpretation.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r5.speaker: الزهري
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r5.claim: Al-Zuhri, in a report transmitted by Ibn Abi Shayba, says al-ma'un means wealth in Quraysh usage.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r6.speaker: أبو عبيدة والزجاج والمبرد
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r6.claim: Abu Ubayda, al-Zajjaj, and al-Mubarrad say the word covered every useful thing, small or large, in pre-Islamic usage, and means obedience in Islam.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r7.speaker: قطرب
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r7.claim: Qutrub derives al-ma'un from ma'n, meaning a small thing, as in the expression for possessing only a little.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r8.speaker: قيل
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r8.claim: Another derivation makes al-ma'un come from ma'una, with the alif replacing the final h and the original form on the maf'al pattern.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r9.speaker: قيل
ALUSI-FULL:v30p242#5/r9.claim: A third derivation treats it as the passive participle of a'ana, with consonant inversion and a later change of waw to alif.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r1.speaker: ابن جريج
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r1.claim: Ibn Jurayj identifies the person as Abu Sufyan: after slaughtering camels, he struck an orphan with his stick when the child asked for meat.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r2.speaker: قيل
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r2.claim: Other identifications are al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, Amr ibn A'id, Manaf, or a miserly hypocrite.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r3.claim: Al-Kashf objects that making the prayer neglecters and show-offs the same defined person does not fit; the author instead reads this as a parenthetical extension from abandoning the orphan to worse conduct.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r4.claim: The passage asks whether deniers and orphan-abandoners behave well or badly, answers that their behavior is bad, then says woe to the praying people to show that they too share these traits.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r5.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r5.claim: Some make the fa in fa-wayl causal, which requires the deniers and praying people to be one group; this supports identifying them as hypocrites, as reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Imam Malik.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r6.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r6.claim: Abu Hayyan objects that the proposed coordination is an unusual construction and that the demonstrative pronoun is awkward and unnecessary, though another says it stresses their remoteness in evil.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r7.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r7.claim: Another analysis coordinates two groups as separate subjects, but al-Kashf objects that the context does not suit a pronoun referring jointly to both and then being replaced by the praying people.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r8.speaker: ابن إسحاق والأشهب
ALUSI-FULL:v30p243/r8.claim: Ibn Ishaq and al-Ashhab read yara'una with a short vowel and a doubled hamza; another transmission from Ibn Ishaq shortens it without doubling.

ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r12.claim: The context includes people who perform a few prayers smugly as if religion consisted only of them, neglecting other duties such as almsgiving and help for God's servants.

ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r13.claim: The Qur'an repeatedly pairs prayer with zakat as foundational righteous duties after faith; some who seem devout wrongly neglect financial obligations.

ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r14.claim: Mosques are maintained by those who believe in God and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakat, and fear only God.

ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r15.speaker: author
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r15.claim: Prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing; people who persist in these and refuse aid have ignored prayer's admonition and meaning.

ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:107:2-7#2/r17.claim: Al-maʿūn may mean zakat, or even the smallest customary loan or assistance; those who withhold such minor help would all the more withhold zakat.

ELMALILI:107:2-7#3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:107:2-7#3/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:107:2-7#3/r1.claim: Religious pretenders who neglect prayer, show off, and withhold even small help are more astonishingly blameworthy than disbelievers who deny religion and mistreat orphans and the poor.

ELMALILI:107:2-7#3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:107:2-7#3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:107:2-7#3/r3.claim: After the address to the Prophet to see and understand, Sūrat al-Kawthar condenses the preceding suras, especially those from al-Ḍuḥā, as a final account of Muhammad's rank.

QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r1.claim: Al-ma'un means aid, kindness, and goodness for fellow human beings and God's servants; withholding it shows prayer's intended effects are absent.

QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r2.claim: If people truly established prayer for God, they would not withhold help from His servants; their treatment of others tests whether worship is sincere and accepted.

QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r3.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r3.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r3.claim: The warned worshippers perform empty motions for show without devotion or effect on their hearts and actions, so their prayer becomes a sin awaiting punishment.

QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r4.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r4.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r4.claim: God's call to faith and worship serves human flourishing, not any need of God: it seeks pure hearts, happiness, mutual care, generosity, love, and brotherhood.

QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r5.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r5.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:107:7/r5.claim: Qutb asks why humanity wanders into dark confusion when divine goodness and mercy offer a clear route to an elevated, generous life.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p568/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p568/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p568/r2.claim: If the surah or its final three verses are Medinan, “those who pray” means hypocrites who only appear to pray; the verb names the appearance of the act, as “the hypocrites fear” means they seem to fear.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p568/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p568/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p568/r3.claim: Al-maʿun here means charity or zakat; the parallel description of hypocrites says they hold back their hands.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p568/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p568/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p568/r4.claim: The causal fa makes the show-praying hypocrites part of the deniers of Judgment who mistreat orphans and fail to urge feeding the poor.

TABATABAI:107:1-7/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:107:1-7/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:107:1-7/r1.claim: The surah warns people professing religion whose traits resemble hypocrites: neglecting prayer, acting ostentatiously, and withholding aid, all incompatible with belief in requital.

TABATABAI:107:1-7/r13.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:107:1-7/r13.speaker: author
TABATABAI:107:1-7/r13.claim: Ma'un is anything that helps another meet a need, such as a loan, a good deed, or lending household goods; this common meaning underlies the different reported definitions.

TABATABAI:107:1-7/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:107:1-7/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:107:1-7/r2.claim: The surah may be Meccan or Medinan; another view says its first half is Meccan and second half Medinan.

TABATABAI:107:5-7/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:107:5-7/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:107:5-7/r4.claim: A Prophetic report identifies ma'un as tools people help each other with, including an axe, cooking pot, bucket, and similar items.

TABATABAI:107:5-7/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:107:5-7/r5.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:107:5-7/r5.claim: A report from Abu Abd Allah defines ma'un as a loan, good deed, household goods lent, and zakat.

TABATABAI:107:5-7/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:107:5-7/r6.speaker: علي عليه السلام
TABATABAI:107:5-7/r6.claim: Sunni reports also explain ma'un as obligatory zakat, connecting prayer-showing with withholding zakat.

TABATABAI:107:5-7/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:107:5-7/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:107:5-7/r7.claim: The Prophet describes ma'un as stone, iron, water, and similar items; another report specifies copper cooking pots and axe iron, and stone pots.

ASAD-NOTES:107:1#n4/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:107:1#n4/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:107:1#n4/r1.claim: Al-ma'un includes small daily-use items and occasional kindnesses that help others with such things.

ASAD-NOTES:107:1#n4/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:107:1#n4/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:107:1#n4/r2.claim: More broadly, al-ma'un means aid or assistance in any difficulty.

ASAD-NOTES:107:intro/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:107:intro/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:107:intro/r1.claim: The surah was revealed in the mission's early years, probably after surah 102; its title comes from al-ma'un in the last verse.

ASAD-NOTES:107:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:107:intro/r2.speaker: some commentators
ASAD-NOTES:107:intro/r2.claim: Some commentators date verses 4–7 to Medina, but Asad rejects this view for lack of historical or textual evidence.

BINTSHATI:v2p189/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p189/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p189/r5.claim: The author treats the next clauses as attached to the inattentive worshippers: riya is showing people an outward state unlike one's inward one, near hypocrisy but also used more broadly.

BINTSHATI:v2p190/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r1.claim: Ma'un can mean water or rain, useful borrowed household items, especially a vessel, or zakat as a small required share withheld from someone in need.

BINTSHATI:v2p190/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r2.claim: Al-Ma'un occurs nowhere else in the Quran.

BINTSHATI:v2p190/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari chooses zakat as the meaning of ma'un.

BINTSHATI:v2p190/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r4.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r4.claim: Most commentators, as al-Razi reports, understand ma'un as ordinary tools people lend each other, such as an axe, bucket, fire striker, salt, water, or fire.

BINTSHATI:v2p190/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r5.claim: The author reports al-Razi's explanation that zakat is called ma'un because one-fortieth is a small amount from much wealth.

BINTSHATI:v2p190/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says refusing to lend such items is legally forbidden in necessity and poor manners otherwise.

BINTSHATI:v2p190/r7.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r7.speaker: الرازي
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r7.claim: Al-Razi calls stinginess over small items base and praises keeping extra household goods to lend beyond the minimum duty.

BINTSHATI:v2p190/r8.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r8.speaker: الطبري
BINTSHATI:v2p190/r8.claim: Al-Tabari combines the readings: people withhold ordinary shared necessities and the needy's required rights in their wealth, all of which are mutual benefits.

BINTSHATI:v2p191/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p191/r1.speaker: بعض المفسرين
BINTSHATI:v2p191/r1.claim: Some commentators limit condemned riya to optional worship, exempting required public duties and acts shown as examples for others.

BINTSHATI:v2p192/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p192/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p192/r2.claim: The verse on righteousness joins prayer and zakat with keeping promises and patience, showing that virtue includes lived faith and care.

BINTSHATI:v2p192/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p192/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p192/r3.claim: The Quran extends responsibility beyond private worship: rejecting the orphan and failing to urge food for the poor counts as denying the religion and neglecting public solidarity and mercy.

CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r3.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r3.claim: The closing verse adds refusal of assistance, generalizing the earlier failure to support orphans and the poor, who represent socially vulnerable people in the Hebrew Bible.

CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r4.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r4.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r4.claim: The two groups cross-correspond: verse 1 and verses 4–6 concern religious omissions, while verses 2–3 and verse 7 concern social omissions; the first group stresses social failings and the second religious ones.

CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r5.claim: Māʿūn and manaʿa are near-anagrams built from permutations of the same consonants, m-n-ʿ and m-ʿ-n.

CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:4-7:kommentar/r6.claim: The rare hapax māʿūn was likely chosen instead of a commoner word for its assonance with manaʿa; the sound pattern sharpens the contrast between expected assistance and its denial, a figure later rhetoricians call reversed paronomasia.

CORPUSCORANICUM:107:7:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:7:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:7:anmerkung/r1.claim: Q 68:12 and 70:21 provide parallels for withholding good or help.

CORPUSCORANICUM:107:7:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:7:anmerkung/r2.speaker: Geiger
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:7:anmerkung/r2.claim: Geiger derives māʿūn from Hebrew māʿôn, meaning dwelling or refuge, and interprets the verse as denying shelter to people seeking help.

CORPUSCORANICUM:107:7:anmerkung/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:7:anmerkung/r3.speaker: Nöldeke
CORPUSCORANICUM:107:7:anmerkung/r3.claim: Nöldeke accepts Geiger's derivation but rejects the assumption that Arabic must preserve the Hebrew word's original meaning.
